source_title: Homejoy at the Unicorn Glue Factory
company_context: Homejoy was a YC-backed on-demand home-cleaning marketplace connecting customers with cleaners. It announced it would shut down effective July 31, 2015. While worker-classification lawsuits were cited by the CEO as the deciding factor, deep reporting documented a severe customer-retention and unit-economics problem underneath.
evidence_summary: Homejoy acquired customers heavily through deep first-cleaning discounts (e.g., $19.99 deals on daily-deal sites) but retained very few. A third-party financial analysis cited by Backchannel showed only about a quarter of customers used the service after the first month and under 10% after six months. The discount-driven funnel attracted customers unwilling to pay full price ($25-35/hour), so high acquisition cost was never recovered. CEO Adora Cheung publicly blamed worker-classification lawsuits and inability to raise more capital.
outcome_evidence: Homejoy announced shutdown effective July 31, 2015. CEO Adora Cheung told Re/code that worker-classification lawsuits were the 'deciding factor' and that the company could not raise enough money to continue; Backchannel documented the underlying retention collapse and customer-acquisition-cost problem.
source_limitations: The Backchannel/Medium article could not be fetched directly in this environment; figures were confirmed verbatim via credible WebSearch snippets. Retention percentages come from a third-party financial analysis 'viewed by Backchannel' rather than an audited company disclosure. The four lawsuits were not class actions.
directly_stated: Only ~25% of customers used the service after the first month; <10% after six months
Deep promotional pricing (e.g., $19.99 first cleanings on daily-deal sites)
Full price $25-35/hour attracted the wrong, price-sensitive customers
Four active worker-classification lawsuits; classification cited as deciding factor
Quote: 'we weren't making enough money on our customers... spending a lot to acquire them, but not really retaining them'
inferred: Negative effective lifetime value: acquisition cost exceeded retained revenue
The legal trigger was the proximate cause, but the retention/CAC structure made the business non-viable regardless
why_useful_for_opsiq: Strong customer_retention_erosion case with a misleading surface narrative (lawsuits) masking the structural cause (retention/CAC). Tests whether a system looks past the founder's stated cause to the cohort-retention data and diagnoses LTV/CAC failure rather than a purely legal shock.
